idiom_name: frozen tagged object literals built by one factory (no static guarantee)
implementation_notes: JavaScript has no type system, so the pattern's guarantee - that an illegal combination cannot be constructed - is simply unavailable: a tagged object can be written by hand anywhere, a switch has no exhaustiveness check, and property access on the wrong variant is a runtime undefined rather than a compile error. What replaces the sealed structure is a two-part discipline: express the union once as JSDoc @typedef union with a literal discriminant and type-check the .js files with // @ts-check or checkJs (the TypeScript checker then narrows on the tag), and validate untrusted input at the boundary with a runtime schema, because JSDoc is not runtime enforcement. Use a single factory plus Object.freeze to make the intended shapes cheap to produce and hard to mutate, and throw from the default branch of every switch so an unexpected variant fails loudly. Prefer the TypeScript realization as soon as the project can adopt it.
pitfalls: Nothing stops a caller from building an object literal with the wrong fields or a wrong tag string: only the factory plus runtime validation at the boundary keeps illegal shapes out, and both are discipline, not enforcement.
A switch over variant strings is never checked for exhaustiveness, so a forgotten case falls into the default branch (or silently returns undefined) unless every switch throws there.
Object.freeze is shallow and JSON.parse/structuredClone happily produce objects with the right tag and missing or extra fields, so re-validate anything crossing the process or network boundary.
alternative: Move the model to TypeScript and express it as a discriminated union on a literal tag (values that do not match a variant do not type-check), or keep JavaScript and run the TypeScript checker over JSDoc @typedef unions with // @ts-check; either way validate untrusted input at the boundary with a runtime schema (Zod, Valibot, Ajv) and let a single factory plus Object.freeze produce the variants, since JavaScript itself enforces nothing at run time.
